transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well… I came in because I just can’t seem to get anything in order anymore. My kitchen table is just covered—my husband’s appointment papers, church flyers, little notes from the senior center, and then my own half-finished lists. I sit down thinking I’ll sort it, and then I don’t know which thing to do first, and somehow the whole day is gone.

It’s funny, I used to keep things in little piles—my mother did that too, though hers were neater—but now the piles don’t mean anything. I just look at them and feel stuck.
Have you been having trouble with your memory?

Yes… I think so. Not like I don’t know who people are or anything, but day-to-day things just slip right past me. I’ve missed returning calls, and bills will be sitting under a stack of mail until I find them much later. My daughter will ask me to run an errand and I’ll say, “Yes, yes, I’ll do it,” and then… it’s gone.

And with my husband’s appointments, that’s been bad. More than once I realized too late that I never called back to confirm one. Then I feel awful, because those papers are usually right there on the table with everything else, but I just don’t seem to follow through.
Were you always this forgetful and disorganized, or is this a change for you?

Oh… no, I suppose it isn’t brand new, not really. I mean, it’s worse now, with all the papers and appointments, but when I think back… even when I was a little girl, my teachers used to write things like, “bright but careless.” I remember that phrase because my mother did not like it.

They’d say I forgot my books, or didn’t turn in homework, or I had to be reminded to finish my seatwork before I could go outside for recess. And of course I’d be looking out the window or thinking about something else… I can still picture that classroom, the big windows and the smell of paste. So, yes, I guess I’ve always had some of that, but it feels much harder to manage now.
Have you been feeling depressed lately?

Depressed… I’m not sure. I wouldn’t say I’ve been sitting around crying, if that’s what you mean. I get discouraged, certainly, especially when I look at all those papers and think, “How did I let it get like this?” But then I’ll think about needing to call my daughter, and then I remember the church newsletter was asking for volunteers—well, I meant to put that somewhere safe, and now I don’t know where it is.

So… I don’t know if I’d call it depressed. More overwhelmed, maybe.
Have you started needing help to manage your bills or appointments?

Yes… well, my daughter has started sort of checking behind me, which I don’t like to admit. She’ll ask, “Mom, did you pay that bill?” or “Did you write down Dad’s appointment?” and then she’ll look at the papers herself because she doesn’t really trust that I’ve kept it all straight.

And I had to give up leading that big event at the senior center—oh, I loved doing that, the one with the tables and the little raffle baskets, and everyone brings those cookies that are too sweet—but there were too many details. I was afraid I’d miss something important, and honestly, I already was missing things. So yes, I guess I am needing help now.
Do you ever get lost in places that should be familiar to you?

Lost? No… I don’t think so. I mean, I might take the wrong turn in a parking lot now and then, especially those big shopping centers where every row looks the same, but I wouldn’t say I get lost in places I know.

Although there was that grocery store they rearranged last year—moved the bread clear across, which I still think was unnecessary—and I wandered around forever looking for the coffee. But that’s not really the same as getting lost, is it? In my own neighborhood or places I’ve been going for years, no, I don’t think so.
Have you been feeling down or sad most days?

Down or sad most days… I don’t know. I wouldn’t say most days, exactly. I have moments where I feel low, especially when things pile up, but then I’ll be thinking about something else entirely, like whether I returned that library book—or no, maybe it was my neighbor’s casserole dish—and it sort of passes.

So… not sad all the time, I don’t think. More like I get worn down sometimes.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot?

Worrying a lot… I’m not sure. I mean, I worry about things the way anyone does, I suppose. Bills and appointments and whether I left something sitting out—well, I guess that’s not exactly what you asked.

My sister used to worry terribly, she’d call me three times before a trip just to ask if she packed her toothbrush, and I always thought, “Goodness, I’m not like that.” But then I do catch myself thinking about little things more than I’d like sometimes.

So… I don’t know if I’d call it a lot. Maybe more when there’s too much going on.
Compared with a few years ago, do you feel your thinking has clearly gotten worse?

Clearly gotten worse… I’m not sure how to answer that. Some days I think, well, I’m 70, nobody’s as quick as they were at 35, right? My mother used to say she kept all her best thinking in her recipe box, which never made sense to me because she lost that box twice.

But compared with a few years ago… I don’t know if I’d say clearly worse. I haven’t really sat down and measured it or anything. I notice little things here and there, but then I think maybe I’ve always been that way. So… I’m not sure.
Because of these thinking and organization problems, have you had to stop managing any important daily tasks on your own?

Well… yes, I suppose I have. I mean, I don’t like saying it that way, because I still feel like I should be able to manage things. I used to help lead this big event at the senior center—there were sign-up sheets and phone calls and making sure the right people brought the right things, you know, all the little pieces. And I finally had to step back from that because I just couldn’t keep it straight anymore.

And my daughter, she’s been… not taking over exactly, but she double-checks my bills and appointments now. She says it’s just to help, but I know it’s because she doesn’t really trust me to keep track of it all by myself. Which is hard to admit.
Has your ability to organize and keep track of things clearly gotten worse recently compared with how you were for most of your adult life?

Yes… I think it has. That’s actually why I came in, really. I can’t seem to get anything in order anymore.

My kitchen table is just… covered. My husband’s appointment papers, church flyers, notes from the senior center, lists I started and didn’t finish—there’s one list on the back of an envelope, which is ridiculous because I bought a perfectly nice notepad for that. And then I sit there looking at all of it, thinking I’ll just pick the most important thing, but I can’t seem to tell which one that is. Then I move a paper from one side to the other, and somehow the whole day goes by.

It feels worse than how I used to be, yes. I wasn’t ever a perfectly tidy person, but I could at least keep track of what needed doing. Now it all piles up and I just sort of freeze.
Have you been having trouble finding the right words when you speak?

I don’t know… not in a way I’ve really noticed, I don’t think. I mean, everyone forgets a word now and then, don’t they? I’ll say “that thing” instead of the name of something, but then my sister does that too, and she’s always been sharp as a tack—well, sharp in some ways, not with directions.

But no, I wouldn’t say I’m sitting there unable to find words all the time. At least, not that I’ve been paying attention to.
Has your daughter told you that your thinking or memory seems worse than it used to be?

Yes… she has, though she tries to say it gently. She’ll say things like, “Mom, let’s just go over this together,” but I know what she means.

After I had to give up helping lead that big senior-center event—you know, the one with all the sign-ups and phone calls and everyone bringing casseroles and coffee urns and such—she started paying closer attention. Now she double-checks my bills and my appointments, and I can tell it’s because she doesn’t really trust me to keep everything straight on my own anymore. I don’t think she means to hurt my feelings, but… yes, she’s noticed.
Do you ever lose track of what day or date it is?

I… I don’t know if I lose track exactly. I mean, I look at the calendar a lot, especially the one on the refrigerator—my daughter bought me one with big squares, very nice, though the pen keeps disappearing, which drives me crazy because I put it right in that little drawer with the rubber bands.

But the day or date… I suppose sometimes I have to check. I wouldn’t say I’m wandering around not knowing what day it is, if that’s what you mean. I just look to make sure.
Have these problems been steadily getting worse over time?

I’m not sure I can say “steadily,” exactly. Some days feel better than others, you know? Like if I sleep well and I’ve had my coffee—though I’m trying not to have it too late because then I’m up watching those old house shows and suddenly it’s midnight.

But… worse over time? I don’t know. My daughter might say yes. I just feel like things come and go, and then when people start watching you more closely, it makes everything seem bigger. I guess I’m not really sure.
Do you ever find yourself not knowing what month it is?

The month? I don’t… I don’t think so. I mean, I know when it’s around Christmas because the stores put things out so early now, it’s ridiculous—Halloween candy right next to ornaments, can you believe that?

But as far as not knowing the month, I usually have some idea. I might look at the calendar to be sure, but I wouldn’t say I’m sitting there thinking it’s March when it’s September or anything like that. At least… not that I’ve noticed.
Do you find yourself repeating the same question or story because you forgot you already said it?

I don’t know… I mean, people say that sometimes, don’t they? “You told me that already.” My daughter says it, but she says it with that little look, and then I feel like—well, maybe I did, maybe I didn’t.

Stories, though… I’ve always told stories. My husband used to say I couldn’t answer a simple question without going around the block first, which, honestly, maybe he had a point. Like there was this neighbor we had who would ask about the tomatoes and then somehow we’d be talking about the post office for twenty minutes.

So I’m not sure if I’m repeating because I forgot, or because I just like talking about something. I don’t really notice it while I’m doing it.
Before the last few years, did these attention and organization problems cause trouble for you throughout most of your adult life?

Oh, before the last few years? Yes, I think so… I mean, it goes way back, really. Even when I was a little girl, my teachers used to write things like, “bright but careless,” which always stung a bit because I wasn’t trying to be careless.

They’d say I forgot my books or my homework, and that I needed reminders to finish my seatwork before I could go outside. I remember that because going outside was a big deal then—we had this blacktop area, and everyone would rush out, and I’d still be sitting there because I hadn’t finished something I thought I’d already done.

So, yes… it wasn’t just recently. It’s kind of been a thread through my life, I suppose.
Would you say your memory and thinking are getting worse month by month?

Month by month? I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I don’t really keep track of it neatly like that—like January I was this way and February was worse.

Some days I feel sharper than other days, you know? And then other times I’ll walk into the kitchen and forget why, but then I think, well, everyone does that. My sister used to say if you don’t write it down, it didn’t happen, and she had little notes everywhere—on the fridge, on the mirror, even one time on the dog food bin, which always made me laugh.

So… getting worse every month? I haven’t noticed it like a steady downhill thing, no. I just don’t know.
Have you been having trouble with planning or carrying out familiar tasks, like cooking a usual meal or following the steps of something you used to do easily?

Yes… I mean, maybe not cooking exactly, though even that can get sideways if I don’t have everything laid out. But the thing that really made me come in was I just can’t seem to get anything in order anymore.

My kitchen table is just—oh, it’s awful—covered with my husband’s appointment papers, church flyers, things from the senior center, little notes I started and didn’t finish. And I sit down thinking, “All right, I’ll take care of this,” but then I don’t know which thing should come first. Like, do I call about the appointment, or put the church paper on the calendar, or finish the grocery list, and then somehow the whole day is gone.

It’s embarrassing, because it’s not like those are strange things. They’re familiar things. I just get stuck in the steps.

I… I don’t know if I lose track exactly. I mean, I look at the calendar a lot, especially the one on the refrigerator—my daughter bought me one with big squares, very nice, though the pen keeps disappearing, which drives me crazy because I put it right in that little drawer with the rubber bands.

But the day or date… I suppose sometimes I have to check. I wouldn’t say I’m wandering around not knowing what day it is, if that’s what you mean. I just look to make sure.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a progressive decline from her lifelong baseline, which would favor a neurocognitive disorder over longstanding ADHD.
doctor.question: Have these problems been steadily getting worse over time?

target_item.reason: The question asks about whether symptoms have been progressively worsening over time, but the provided symptom profile only covers ADHD symptoms, onset, duration, and impairment—not a steady worsening or progressive course.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I can say “steadily,” exactly. Some days feel better than others, you know? Like if I sleep well and I’ve had my coffee—though I’m trying not to have it too late because then I’m up watching those old house shows and suddenly it’s midnight.

But… worse over time? I don’t know. My daughter might say yes. I just feel like things come and go, and then when people start watching you more closely, it makes everything seem bigger. I guess I’m not really sure.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is evidence of impaired orientation to time, which would support a neurocognitive disorder over lifelong ADHD.
doctor.question: Do you ever find yourself not knowing what month it is?

target_item.reason: The question asks about orientation to time (not knowing what month it is), which is not covered by the listed ADHD symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
The month? I don’t… I don’t think so. I mean, I know when it’s around Christmas because the stores put things out so early now, it’s ridiculous—Halloween candy right next to ornaments, can you believe that?

But as far as not knowing the month, I usually have some idea. I might look at the calendar to be sure, but I wouldn’t say I’m sitting there thinking it’s March when it’s September or anything like that. At least… not that I’ve noticed.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a progressive decline in recent memory beyond lifelong inattentiveness, which would favor major neurocognitive disorder over ADHD.
doctor.question: Do you find yourself repeating the same question or story because you forgot you already said it?

target_item.reason: The question is about repetitive questioning or storytelling due to forgetting having already said it, which is not specifically covered by the listed ADHD symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I don’t know… I mean, people say that sometimes, don’t they? “You told me that already.” My daughter says it, but she says it with that little look, and then I feel like—well, maybe I did, maybe I didn’t.

Stories, though… I’ve always told stories. My husband used to say I couldn’t answer a simple question without going around the block first, which, honestly, maybe he had a point. Like there was this neighbor we had who would ask about the tomatoes and then somehow we’d be talking about the post office for twenty minutes.

So I’m not sure if I’m repeating because I forgot, or because I just like talking about something. I don’t really notice it while I’m doing it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether inattention/disorganization has been present across adulthood before recent decline, which best separates lifelong ADHD from a new neurocognitive disorder.
doctor.question: Before the last few years, did these attention and organization problems cause trouble for you throughout most of your adult life?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even as a little girl, my teachers wrote that I was bright but careless, forgot books and homework, and needed reminders to finish seatwork before I could go outside.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the attention and organization problems were long-standing before recent years, which most directly relates to early onset of symptoms.

patient.answer:
Oh, before the last few years? Yes, I think so… I mean, it goes way back, really. Even when I was a little girl, my teachers used to write things like, “bright but careless,” which always stung a bit because I wasn’t trying to be careless.

They’d say I forgot my books or my homework, and that I needed reminders to finish my seatwork before I could go outside. I remember that because going outside was a big deal then—we had this blacktop area, and everyone would rush out, and I’d still be sitting there because I hadn’t finished something I thought I’d already done.

So, yes… it wasn’t just recently. It’s kind of been a thread through my life, I suppose.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is evidence of a progressive decline from her longstanding attention problems, which would favor a neurocognitive disorder over lifelong ADHD alone.
doctor.question: Would you say your memory and thinking are getting worse month by month?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about progressive worsening of memory and thinking over time, which suggests cognitive decline; none of the listed ADHD symptom profile items specifically cover month-by-month worsening cognition.

patient.answer:
Month by month? I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I don’t really keep track of it neatly like that—like January I was this way and February was worse.

Some days I feel sharper than other days, you know? And then other times I’ll walk into the kitchen and forget why, but then I think, well, everyone does that. My sister used to say if you don’t write it down, it didn’t happen, and she had little notes everywhere—on the fridge, on the mirror, even one time on the dog food bin, which always made me laugh.

So… getting worse every month? I haven’t noticed it like a steady downhill thing, no. I just don’t know.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is clear impairment in a second cognitive domain beyond attention/organization, which would support a neurocognitive disorder over lifelong ADHD.
doctor.question: Have you been having trouble with planning or carrying out familiar tasks, like cooking a usual meal or following the steps of something you used to do easily?

target_item.name: Organization_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I can’t seem to get anything in order anymore—my kitchen table is covered with my husband’s appointment papers, church flyers, senior-center notes, and half-finished lists, and I sit there not knowing which thing to do first until the whole day is gone.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about trouble planning and carrying out familiar multi-step tasks, which most directly matches difficulty organizing tasks and activities.

patient.answer:
Yes… I mean, maybe not cooking exactly, though even that can get sideways if I don’t have everything laid out. But the thing that really made me come in was I just can’t seem to get anything in order anymore.

My kitchen table is just—oh, it’s awful—covered with my husband’s appointment papers, church flyers, things from the senior center, little notes I started and didn’t finish. And I sit down thinking, “All right, I’ll take care of this,” but then I don’t know which thing should come first. Like, do I call about the appointment, or put the church paper on the calendar, or finish the grocery list, and then somehow the whole day is gone.

It’s embarrassing, because it’s not like those are strange things. They’re familiar things. I just get stuck in the steps.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a lifelong pattern of inattention and disorganization beginning in childhood, with teacher comments such as 'bright but careless,' forgetting books/homework, and needing reminders to finish seatwork. These symptoms persisted through adult life and are now causing significant impairment in managing bills, appointments, and community responsibilities. Although she also describes some worsening in recent years, the interview does not establish a clear progressive global cognitive decline, disorientation, aphasia, or steadily worsening course sufficient to support F09 over a chronic attentional/executive disorder. The presentation is most consistent with ADHD, predominantly inattentive type.
